In a 2019 interview, Siegel described working as a chef at Craft in New York after culinary school, then entering the family real estate business before becoming an angel investor and venture capitalist. The interview does not identify the relatives or name the family business. [8]

In a 2017 interview, he said a family death and an illness affecting another relative led him to close his real estate development company in 2007. The relatives were not identified. He described founding Georgetown Angels with Andrew Romans, whom he met at Georgetown in 1998, and developing it into Rubicon Venture Capital. A 2013 SEC submission independently identifies Siegel as co-chairman of Georgetown Angels. [9, 10]

Investments and board activity

His published investment experience includes Daily Harvest, Super Coffee, Superhuman, Penny, Confiant, EasyKnock, TodayTix, Easyship and Bespoke Post. Acronym lists director roles at Mad Rabbit, Marqii and Penny, and observer roles at Confiant, Dataplor, Envoy America, Ingest, Kickfin, Ranktify and Sailes. Family information and limits

Joshua and Laura Wedding

Identification: Laura’s explicit LinkedIn marriage statement, Emory’s use of Joshua’s middle initial, the matching wedding date and place, and the culinary background provide strong corroboration that these sources describe the same couple. [6, 11, 13, 14]

No publicly available photograph of their chuppah was located.

📊 Decoding the Percentages: Equity and “Skin in the Game”

Because Patriot is a privately held private equity firm, it is not legally mandated to publish an exact, dollar-for-dollar equity split of its management company. However, regulatory disclosures filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) provide two precise lenses into how the money and power are distributed:

1. The 25% to 50% Management Bracket

Under the firm’s regulatory Form ADV Schedule A filings, the SEC groups Wycoff, Lynch, and Lubert together as the primary “Control Persons.” In this institutional framework, the trio splits the foundational voting power, falling into the 25% to 50% individual ownership bracket of the overarching management firm. 2. The 1% to 5% GP Capital Commitment

Beyond managing outside institutional money, the founders are contractually required to have their own personal wealth locked up in the funds. Known in private equity as the General Partner (GP) Commitment, Wycoff, Lynch, and Lubert collectively pledge between 1% and 5% of the total fund size out of their own pockets. Important Canadian Ownership Restriction

RBC is subject to Canadian banking-law ownership restrictions.

The proxy explains that shares cannot be voted by a person who has acquired more than 10% of a class of RBC shares without approval from Canada’s Minister of Finance.

This makes RBC structurally different from a company where one billionaire, family, or hedge fund can simply accumulate a controlling 20%, 30%, or 50% position.

3. BlackRock

Rather:

BlackRock investment entities/client accounts → roughly 5% interest in RBC → RBC owns City National Bank.

That is an indirect economic interest, not direct ownership or control of City National.

No.

Marcia Sue Amster Heller was born in Cleveland on Dec. 17, 1949, and was raised in University Heights by her late parents, Eugene and Sonia Amster. She passed away in Los Angeles, Calif., Jan. 23, 2026.

Marcia was the dearly beloved wife of Jack Heller, the devoted mother of Samuel (Erin Dorman-Heller) Heller and grandmother to their puppy, Luca, the dear sister of Howard Amster and Terry Nussbaum and the sister-in-law of Tammy Gould.

Marcia graduated from Cleveland Heights High School in 1967 and attended The Ohio State University in Columbus, graduating in 1971 with a degree in microbiology. She met the love of her life, Jack, at The Ohio State University Hillel and they were married in Cleveland on June 25, 1972. Marcia finished her Master’s of Science degree in microbiology at Cleveland State University and worked in a research capacity as a microbiologist at Cleveland Clinic.

In 1979, Jack and Marcia moved to Pasadena, Calif., where their son, Samuel Jacob Heller, was born in 1980. Driven by a mother’s fierce love and a desire to provide Samuel with the best possible support for his development, Marsha pivoted her career, becoming a dedicated speech pathologist. This move was not just a career change, but a calling that allowed her to merge her scientific background with her innate desire to nurture and advocate for others.

She was a pillar of her community and a tireless philanthropist. Her heart was particularly tethered to causes involving hearing health, Israel and Jewish continuity. She was the driving force behind pioneering hearing missions in Mexico and Israel, specifically designed to aid orphans. Through these missions, she ensured that children in need received essential hearing tests and life-changing hearing aids.

Her devotion to Judaism was the heartbeat of her home. She was an avid genealogical researcher, meticulously documenting her family histories and organizing family reunions and gatherings. Sukkot held a special place in her heart. She found immense joy in the hospitality of the holiday, hosting friends and family for lively gatherings under the sukkah.

Marcia Amster Heller lived a life that blended a sharp scientific mind with a soft, empathetic heart. She taught us that the greatest use of one’s intelligence is in the service of those who need a voice.

A funeral service was held Jan. 30 at Hillcrest Memorial Park in Bedford Heights.

Kauffman is ready for the challenge

Joe Callahan Staff writer

Dec. 7, 2014, 4:39 p.m. ET

Bill Kauffman chose Ocala as his hometown 17 years ago because he wanted to live in a quality, family-friendly community.

And now Kauffman, 49, plans to keep improving Marion County through his role as interim county administrator, hoping to one day retire in the community he loves so much.

Kauffman knows his leadership will be closely watched during the next nine months. It’s a tryout of sorts as he works to drop the “interim” part of his title.

Kauffman replaces Lee Niblock, who left to take the same job in Alachua County. At first, the County Commission wanted to conduct a national search to find a successor. But the commission ultimately promoted Kauffman from assistant administrator of public and administrative services to the new post, with a healthy salary increase, from $108,576 to $157,500.

By September, if Kauffman succeeds, he will get a five-year contract. Kauffman said he’s ready for the challenge and has a top-quality executive team in place.

A few weeks ago at a commission meeting, commissioners suddenly ditched the idea of a national search and asked if Kauffman — who had been “acting” county administrator for a few weeks — wanted to take on the nine-month challenge.

“I’m excited about the opportunity,” said Kauffman, adding he was not fazed by the sudden jump into the position.

Kauffman said county government’s top priorities are public safety and infrastructure, such as roads. He said the big focus will be on trying to find funding for public safety, especially to satisfy the Sheriff’s Office’s and Marion Fire Rescue’s needs.

“Now that we finally have come out of the Great Recession, we can start forecasting much farther out now,” said Kauffman, adding that he will be working with his team to develop a five-year plan.

He said that over time, primarily through attrition, he wants to streamline government. He wants to review each department to find better ways to operate and, at the same time, improve customer service — all under the direction of the County Commission. The county has 1,400 employees.

It was 1997 when Kauffman became administrator of Shands HomeCare, where he was responsible for overseeing businesses in nine counties. He could have chosen a town in any of those counties, but felt that Marion County was the place to raise a family.

“Quality of life,” Kauffman said. “That was what we were looking for when we came to Ocala.”

Kauffman grew up in rural Etters, Pennsylvania, with a population of fewer than 1,000. He lived across the highway from his grandparents’ 100-acre farm.

In 1984 he married his childhood sweetheart, Cindy, whom he met in high school after his family moved to Tampa. The move coincidentally occurred after the Three Mile Island nuclear reactor meltdown nearby.

In Tampa, he attended Tampa Technical High School his first two years and then A.P. Leto Comprehensive High School and Temple Heights Christian School, where he graduated in 1983.

After high school graduation, he purchased and operated his own ice cream business until he finally decided to enroll at the University of South Florida. That’s where he earned a bachelor’s degree in business administration in 1993. He later earned a master’s degree in business administration from Kennedy Western University in 2004.

Kauffman joined Marion County in 2008 as an assistant county administrator. From 2002 to 2008 he was chief financial officer for Hospice of Marion County.

He was a reimbursement manager for UF Health Shands Hospital in Gainesville from 1999-2002, and director of operations and then administrator of Shands HomeCare from 1997-99. He worked as a controller and general manager in the private sector in the 1980s.

Kauffman said he has more than just a strong financial background. He has proven leadership abilities, including six years as an assistant county administrator.

Barbara Fitos, a former Marion County commissioner who worked with Kauffman when she was a commissioner from 2006-10, said he has had wonderful mentors in former county administrators Patrick Howard and Niblock.

“It’s a challenging and daunting task,” Fitos noted. “I wish him all the best.”

She said to be successful he needs to “pull together his team of deputy administrators and department heads … collectively they have an amazing depth of knowledge and expertise — leverage that.”

Since 1997, Kauffman — who played football in high school — has coached his children’s sports teams, including baseball. He loves family involvement and is a devout Christian. All of his children — Billy, 20, Kimmy, 18, and Joey, 16 — attended Ocala Christian Academy. Billy and Kimmy are now in college.

Kauffman said he will be looking to local “business family” to help the community grow and prosper — creating a community that will keep young people wanting to come back after college graduation.

“I want my kids to come back here,” said Kauffman, who says he plans to work in Marion County until his retirement.
